text: Beyond the general harvest-glut price dip, two more specific seasonal patterns are worth a Preah Vihear farmer knowing when deciding when to sell. First, demand for some products rises around major Khmer holidays -- particularly Khmer New Year (Choul Chnam Thmey, mid-April) and Pchum Ben (typically September/October) -- when household spending on food and livestock for ceremonies and family gatherings increases. This can create a temporary local demand bump, but a farmer should not assume it always translates into a meaningfully higher price without checking current local conditions, since supply timing, transport access, and other sellers' behavior around the same holiday also affect the actual outcome. Second, livestock sales are affected by a timing conflict specific to the dry season (រដូវប្រាំង, roughly November-April): as forage becomes scarce and grazing fails later in the dry season, farmers can be forced to sell cattle before they've reached good market weight simply because feed can no longer sustain them -- an underweight, distress sale rather than a planned one. This is a real structural conflict: the dry season can be both a period of rising food demand (approaching the new wet-season planting cycle) and a period when a farmer's own animals are in their weakest condition to sell well. Where a farmer can plan ahead -- by conserving dry-season feed earlier, as covered in cattle basic-care guidance -- avoiding a forced underweight sale is usually more valuable than trying to time a sale for a holiday demand bump. For crops like rice and cashew, holding stock to sell later usually requires proper drying and storage capacity that many smallholders lack, so waiting for a better price must be weighed honestly against real storage losses and the farmer's actual cash needs, not assumed to always be the better choice. Do not assume a specific price premium exists around any holiday without current local verification.
